1:
Whether the opening word is a cry of woe or a summons is settled the same way by three. Gill notes that the term is vocative and that the Greek renders it as an address, O bloody city; Ellicott renders it so without argument. Calvin calls the exclamation emphatic and reads it as though the prophet were constraining the city to undergo its punishment. Keil and Delitzsch keep the woe and use it to mark the structure of what follows: the city has brought this fate on itself, can no more avert it than a great Egyptian city could, and comes at last to a terrible end.

The two nouns describing the city are handled quite differently. Keil and Delitzsch treat them as accusatives without a conjunction, the first meaning deceit. Calvin observes that one signifies leanness and the other to lay by, and argues that the prophet has joined two words which seem to differ widely and yet mean the same, both denoting spoil: the city was full of leanness because it had consumed all others and of plunder because it had filled itself. On the clause about the prey Calvin reports the reading that it shall not be withdrawn from the conquerors' hands but prefers the other, a continued licence in plundering; Henry reaches the same sense plainly, that they never knew when they had got enough.

Henry draws the whole into an indictment of five counts, and neither numbers nor grandeur will secure the place from prosecution: blood shed by unrighteous war or under colour of justice; lies, so that no man knows whom to trust; rapine, nobody caring what mischief he does or to whom; idolatries, by which she defiled herself and seduced her neighbours; and witchcrafts, by which, aiming at universal monarchy, she used arts as well as arms and courted other nations into her rites. For this God has a quarrel with her, since he who made of one blood all nations never designed one to be a nation of tyrants and another of slaves.

The battle picture of the next two verses is taken by most as the enemy's entry. Ellicott renders it as exclamations, hark to the whip and to the rattling wheel, the horse galloping and the chariot bounding: the entry of the victorious besiegers. Keil and Delitzsch have the prophet see the hostile army burst upon the city and hear the charioteers' whips. Gill makes the whip that of a driver urging his horses to reach the city, heard by the inhabitants and so the more terrible; Wesley identifies the horsemen as the Chaldeans and their confederates. Clarke turns the passage into a rhapsody, hearing the whip crack and the wheels rumble, seeing the chariots bound after the galloping steeds, the spears like gashes of lightning, and the slain in heaps with horses stumbling over them, then breaking off to call war infernal and add that it is sometimes the scourge of the Lord.

Calvin alone reads those verses the other way. He reports that interpreters are divided, some taking the description of the Chaldean army after it had invaded and others of the state of the city in the prophet's own day, and judges the second more consistent with the order of the poem, the sacking having already been set out. He offers his own version, deriving one verb from a root meaning to feel after a thing in order to explore it, reading one phrase as a multitude dancing or piping against the dead mass of the slain, and proposing that a letter in another word is a copyist's mistake. On the flaming sword he is briefer: the word means a flame, and though the brightness of blades is often taken for it metaphorically, since the prophet says in the same breath that the spears lighten he does not doubt the swords flame.
4:
The harlot is taken by all as idolatry and by two as more. Clarke notes that the city was figured a moment ago as a lion tearing all in pieces and is now a beautiful prostitute enticing all men into idolatry and so into the same wrath. Wesley allows both senses, the idolatries multiplied by the many peoples who served the Assyrian gods, and literal whoredom too, which he says abounded where wealth and luxury were found; he glosses the witchcrafts as bewitching policies or the necromancy that flourished there, and the families as eminent houses seduced into an hereditary service of those gods, the devil there imitating God's own institution. Gill pursues the epithet into the name of the city, which two scholars derive from a word for a pleasant habitation, agreeing with its situation on the river; and he recalls that the queen from whose husband it is thought to be named was first a harlot of surpassing beauty.

Calvin makes the change of speaker at the fifth verse the point, as at the close of the last chapter. God testifies that the Assyrians have no strife with any mortal but with their own judgment: they need not measure their forces against the Chaldeans, who do not break in of themselves but are guided by a hidden providence to execute a sentence passed. The title of hosts, he adds, belongs to the circumstance, God declaring his power so they should not think escape possible.

The stripping is explained by three from a public custom. Clarke says it was an ancient though not a laudable practice to strip such women or throw their clothes over their heads and expose them to public execration; Wesley reads it as the treatment inhuman soldiers give captive women. Calvin turns the figure the other way: a harlot is finely dressed and adds disguises, so her dress conceals what she is, but throw the clothes over her head and the beauty is gone; so God will strip the city of the magnificence that has blinded her and dazzled all nations. On the filth cast at her Gill and Clarke point to the same custom, the dirt thrown at women set in the pillory or carted. Calvin generalises it: God besprinkles kingdoms with defilement when he casts them down, since then everyone begins to speak freely and those who lately pretended admiration bring out reproaches.

One word at the end of that verse sets Calvin against the received rendering. Some, he reports, take it for dung or something fetid, one version so rendering it; but since the word comes from the verb to see, those are more correct who make it a spectacle, and he cites an ancient translator and the Greek, which renders it an example. The common English rendering of a gazing-stock he judges less proper. He adds why the city should be an example at all: its ruin was more memorable than any before. Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke keep the gazing-stock without comment.

Why nobody bewails her divides them again. Clarke and Wesley answer from her deserts, that she was the occasion of ruin to multitudes and is now deservedly exposed, Wesley asking whose bowels will be moved for her that had none for anyone. Ellicott adds a reason for the flight, that men run from the stricken city lest they share her punishment, and that one whose cruelties were as wide as her empire is no object of compassion; he closes with two lines of verse on the fallen tyrant left to groan unpitied and alone. Calvin reports that reading and doubts it: he is not sure so refined a meaning came into the prophet's mind, and prefers the simpler sense, that the ruin of so splendid a city would be no ordinary one, and were its greatness duly weighed, though all the world wept, no lamentation would equal it.
8:
Which Egyptian city is meant is the chief question, and three answers are given. Wesley and Calvin proceed as though it were Alexandria, and Gill reports the Targum and three Jewish commentators taking it so; but Gill leans the other way, to the great city of the south famous in the old poet for its hundred gates, noting that some think that number was not of gates but of temples. Ellicott names the same southern capital and explains the Hebrew form as the house of the god whose name it carries. Clarke puts it in the Delta instead, on one branch of the river: it had the fork of two branches to defend it by land and the sea for a barrier, so the place was wholly surrounded by water.

When the city fell, and to whom, is equally unsettled. Clarke supposes it destroyed lately, probably by the Chaldeans. Gill reports one Jewish authority that the Chaldean king took it on his way to Nineveh, remarks that when and by whom is nowhere said, and cites two chronologers who assign the sack to the Assyrian king who harassed Egypt three years together. Ellicott alone marshals the Assyrian records, listing three campaigns with their dates: a defeat of the Egyptian commander in the field, a later king's rout of the Ethiopian ruler, and a third invasion in which the city was sacked and a booty of gold, silver, captives and obelisks carried to Nineveh. From that he draws a conclusion nobody else attempts: the fall being already past when the prophet wrote, the allusion helps fix the date of the book.

What the comparison is for they understand alike, and two press it hardest. Henry takes the prophet to be quoting precedents to break a false confidence, the city having said in effect that she should have peace, and draws the moral that it keeps us in a holy fear to consider we are no better than those who fell before us. Ellicott builds the argument clause by clause. To human reasoning the fall of the southern capital testified to the power of the conqueror; to the prophet's vision the ruin of one world-power is an earnest of the other's, both being full of luxury and oppression and both hated of mankind. If the one city was protected by its rivers, had not the other a rampart in the great river and its canals; if the one relied on friendly states, had not the other all the resources of Africa.

The allies are counted up by four with small differences. Henry adds the trade as well as the auxiliary troops, and calls the place fortified by nature and art at once, the river both watering the fields and guarding the wall. Clarke locates the further two peoples in Africa and Libya, within reach of forming alliances; Wesley makes one the Moors west of Alexandria and glosses the boast of infinite strength as meaning there was no end to their confidence and provision. Keil and Delitzsch render the two verses through and state the moral in a line, that the fate of the one city is a prophecy of the other's.

The treatment of the captives is where Calvin dwells longest. He takes the dashing of the children as a barbarity that spared what its own tenderness should have protected, since infants could not be reckoned enemies; and the prophet records it, he says, so that Nineveh should not trust her strength and despise the judgment denounced. On the casting of lots he explains the ancient practice, that when two captors disputed a prisoner the lot decided whose he should be; what is remarkable is that lots were cast on the princes, a thing usually reserved for the lowest slaves. Clarke reports the same custom, and the great men kept in chains to grace the triumph.
11:
Calvin makes the little word also carry the argument. The cup is a familiar figure for punishment, and to be made drunk with it marks a severe one, the city lying stupefied like a man overcome with wine; but the particle is emphatic, put in so the Ninevites should know they could not escape what they deserved. God, he says, continues ever like himself and is judge of the world to the end, so having punished the Egyptian city he cannot leave the Assyrian exempt.

What it means that she shall be hid is disputed in the same verse. Calvin reports the reading that refers it to shame, a proud city driven by calamity to seek hiding-places; but he inclines rather to think she would vanish away as though she had never been, since to be hidden is often taken in Hebrew for being reduced to nothing.

On the figs they are of one mind and differ only in what they draw. Gill and Wesley note that the first ripe fruit is loosened by the least shake, so the fortresses they trusted in would fall as easily. Clarke turns the metaphor into history: at the first shock all the strongholds were abandoned and the king in despair burnt himself and his household in his palace. Calvin generalises it into a doctrine: whatever strength men gather will vanish, since neither forts nor towers nor troops avail anything, and were nobody to rise against them they would still fall of themselves.

Whether the people are called women for their manners or their fright divides two sharply. Gill reads it of a settled character, a people weak and timorous, fleeing at the first approach of the enemy, with some regard, he thinks, to their king's effeminacy. Ellicott denies exactly that: the phrase has nothing to do with the luxurious habits an excavator reports of them, but refers to their panic at the catastrophe, when they found the avenues laid open and the defences burning. Wesley calls them cowards and takes the gates for the frontier fortresses, opened by fear or treachery.

That the advice which follows is ironical is agreed, and Ellicott explains how it works. The city is scoffingly told to protract her resistance: the outer walls are down, so let her hold out in the citadel, lay in water and build new buttresses of brick; and in the middle of those preparations fire and sword will surprise her. He observes that the account of the last struggle is minute on purpose, and compares another prophet who, describing the making of an idol, goes back to the smith at his tongs and the carpenter at his rule; in both the irony gains force from minute description of useless operations. Gill says the same briefly, that they might do what they would and it would all be in vain.

Clarke is the only one who has handled the materials. He explains that the river ran near, so they are told to lay in fresh water against a long siege, and describes the ancient brickmaking of that country, the clay dug and kneaded by treading, mixed with straw, moulded and dried in the sun; and adds that he has some of those very bricks before him as he writes, hard yet wholly soluble in water, with others made without straw that appear kiln-burnt. Calvin keeps to the words and rejects one construction: to take the verb as meaning to hold or lay hold is wholly foreign to the prophet's meaning, and what is intended is the joining of the bricks into a solid building, since buildings often fall for want of being well joined; the country, he notes, had little stone and supplied the want with brick. Keil and Delitzsch render the verses through and say the prophet is taking away the last prop of the city's hope, its fortifications and its numbers.
15:
Calvin makes the adverb of place carry the sting of the fifteenth verse. The point is not that the labour would be wasted but that the Lord would turn the very defences they trusted in to their destruction: though the soldiers were content with water from cisterns and the walls carefully joined, their frugality and care would not merely fail but turn to their ruin, since God pronounces accursed the arrogance of men who trust their own resources. Gill leaves the fire open, taking it for the fire of divine wrath, or what the enemy would put in, or, with a Jewish commentator and the Targum, the enemy himself. Wesley fixes it in the fortresses and turns the challenge back: let them be as many as they can, it will be to no purpose.

The locusts are natural history to two of them. Clarke refers the reader to his notes on an earlier prophet for the creatures in their various states, calls the successive swarms the most expressive simile for the successive armies, and says they shelter about the hedges in cold weather and forage in the heat. Ellicott says the three insect words stand for varieties of one species, and explains the behaviour the other way about, a burst of sunshine sending a swarm into flight while cold makes them settle and takes from them the power of flying.

Gill goes furthest from the text at that verse. He canvasses who the crowned are, tributary kings distinguished by their headgear, or the city's princes in their coronets, or its priests; then leaves the exposition to establish that locusts really do wear crowns. Some have been seen with little crowns on their heads; a swarm out of the Turkish provinces into Austria and Silesia wore them; an ancient writer speaks of locusts in Arabia marked with gold-coloured figures; and the Targum mentions a shining locust like gold.

Ellicott keeps to the offices instead. The crowned are the subordinate kings who represented the empire in its provinces, the word rendered captains is an Assyrian term for a high military rank, the shepherds are chief officers, and the clause about the nobles should read not that they shall dwell but that they lie still. Wesley agrees that the crowned are confederate kings whose number was all for show.

Who the last Assyrian king was Gill alone tries to settle, by an argument from the historians. One name is the last the Scriptures give; a Greek historian ends the monarchy with a second; another makes a third king reign when the city fell. Gill takes the second and third for the same man, set far apart by different hands, since the same things are told of both, particularly that each burnt himself and his household in the palace when he saw his danger; and it is improbable, he adds, that the same city should have been destroyed twice by the same peoples, those who tell of the one saying nothing of the other.

The slumbering shepherds are explained by three. Calvin takes them for the counsellors in whose wisdom the king trusted, and finds that confidence ridiculed, since these had not vigilance enough to take care even of themselves; he notes that the verb stands in the past either to mark the certainty of the prediction or by the common change of tense, and disputes another verb, holding that a letter in it has been altered. Clarke makes them the rulers and tributary princes who deserted the city in her distress, and supports it from the historians: many nations revolted to the besiegers for the sake of liberty while the king sent to his provinces for help, believing he could endure the siege because an oracle had said the city would not fall till the river turned enemy. Keil and Delitzsch render the verses and sum up the kingdom's end in a line.
19:
Why the ruin should be incurable is answered by Calvin before it is described. The wicked, he says, cannot escape calamity, yet they harbour false expectations and think they will soon gather new strength; the prophet speaks as he does to take that hope away. Gill reaches the same point historically, the blow given by the taking of the city being irreparable, since the place was no more and the empire never rose again.

The word for the wound divides them, and Calvin names the rendering he rejects. Gill offers two: either there is no healing of the bruise, or no contraction of it, as when a wound is nearly closed and the skin round about is wrinkled and drawn together. Calvin dismisses that second sense outright, saying that some render the word a wrinkle but improperly. His own account is that the term is used elsewhere both of restraining men's wickedness and of checking the spread of leprosy, so what is denied here is any stopping of the breach short of its becoming complete; the ancient Greek, he notes, gives simply that there is no healing to the breach, and he calls the figure striking, the fall of the city being a wound that cannot be seamed up. On the clause that follows he would read not that the wound is grievous but that the stroke is, deriving the verb from a root meaning to be languid, so that the pain of the stroke cannot be allayed.

The clapping of hands is read as rejoicing by four and as something slightly different by one. Clarke and Wesley take it plainly for exultation over the downfall, Wesley adding that the wickedness meant is the tyranny, pride and cruelty by which she trod her neighbours down. Ellicott makes the joy universal and asks the question that justifies it, where her oppressive rule had not been felt; he observes too that the verse is addressed to the king himself, in the second person masculine, as representative of the empire and perhaps with his own terrible end in view. Calvin allows the common rendering but suggests another: many take a singular for a plural and make it the clapping of hands, yet since striking the hand is in Hebrew a token of consent, it would not be unsuitable to understand that wherever the report was heard all would express approbation of the judgment.

What the cruelty consisted in Ellicott alone illustrates, and he does it from the monuments rather than the text. Quoting a modern writer, he points to the sculptures as the record of that government: the rows of the impaled, the prisoners with rings fastened through their lips, those whose eyes were put out, those flayed alive. It would be a joy to all nations, on that showing, to hear the tyrant's messengers no more.

Clarke closes the chapter with a long quotation on the improbability of what happened. What likelihood was there, his authority asks, that the capital of a great kingdom should be totally destroyed, a city sixty miles in compass, with walls a hundred feet high and thick enough for three chariots abreast, and fifteen hundred towers of two hundred feet? Yet it was so totally destroyed that the place is hardly known where it stood. What helped to complete the devastation, he suggests, was the enlarging of Babylon soon after the capture; from that time the sacred writers make no mention of the city, and the most ancient heathen authors who speak of it treat it as one once great and flourishing and now desolate. So little remains that writers are not agreed even about its situation, the general suffrage of the older historians placing it on one river while others put it on another. Keil and Delitzsch render the verse through without comment, and Gill notes only what the Targum makes of it.
